cases.abstract: To collect manipulation data across varied scenes while preserving reproducible control, DROID combines a distributed dataset with a portable platform shared by 13 institutions. Common Franka Panda hardware standardizes control, while portability, randomized task assignment, and prompts to vary cameras, lighting, clutter, or robot placement broaden scene coverage. The dataset contains 76,000 successful episodes with language annotations; unsuccessful trajectories are also released but excluded from co-training. Existing diffusion policies are trained separately for six tasks in four locations, comparing in-domain-only training with equal-part co-training using either DROID or a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture under the same backbone. DROID co-training exceeds the next-best method in mean success by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 percentage points under task-specific distribution shifts. An equal-size subset comparison also favors broader scene diversity on the challenging shifted tasks studied. These findings support DROID as a supplementary training resource for the evaluated tasks on its collection hardware.
cases.methods: DROID makes distributed collection reproducible through a shared, portable Franka Panda platform with two external stereo cameras, a wrist stereo camera, and VR teleoperation. Collectors calibrate cameras in each new scene and enter feasible tasks, which are randomly assigned for individual episodes. Periodic prompts change camera placement, lighting, clutter, or base position to broaden coverage rather than concentrate on easy tasks. Crowdsourcing associates episodes with up to three independent language instructions. Training utility is tested with separate language-conditioned diffusion policies for six tasks across four locations on the same hardware. Using a common backbone, policies receive either in-domain demonstrations alone or a 50/50 mixture with successful DROID trajectories or curated Open X-Embodiment data. Each method and task setting receives ten rollouts, covering perturbed in-distribution starts and task-specific shifts in objects, distractors, or cameras.
cases.results: Co-training with DROID improves the mean success rate of existing diffusion policies across six tasks in four locations on DROID hardware. With a common backbone and a 50/50 mixture of in-domain and successful DROID trajectories, it exceeds the next-best method by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 percentage points on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. The comparison includes in-domain-only training and equal-part co-training with a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture, with ten rollouts per method and task setting. A separate comparison uses 7,362 successful demonstrations per subset in 50/50 in-domain co-training: a uniformly sampled, more scene-diverse subset performs better than one from the 20 most represented scenes on the challenging shifted tasks studied. This count-matched result supports a role for scene diversity beyond demonstration quantity, although other subset differences are not fully isolated. The gains support its utility as a supplement to in-domain data within these tasks and scene changes.

notes.abstract: Selected D01-D03 (Section III) to connect reproducible collection with scene variation, and D05-D08 (Section V) to establish supplementary training utility. Read-back retains both dataset and platform, identifies the matched-backbone comparison, and limits the gains to task-specific co-training on DROID hardware.
notes.methods: Selected D01-D03 and D05-D07 to explain how collection variation feeds a controlled policy comparison. Read-back preserves randomized feasible tasks, successful-trajectory co-training, and ten rollouts per method and task setting; it does not assign that rollout count to the diversity comparison.
notes.results: Selected D06-D08 (Section V; Figs. 8 and 10) to distinguish training utility from scene-composition evidence. Read-back keeps the next-best comparator unspecified, reports percentage-point differences rather than relative gains, and treats the equal-size subset result as support for diversity without isolating every confound.

cases.abstract: SIMPLER provides a simulated evaluation framework for robot policies trained on real data, targeting relative performance rather than exact real-world success rates. Its design addresses two discrepancies that can affect these comparisons: controller action effects and visual appearance. Actions from existing real demonstrations guide controller tuning to reduce simulated trajectory mismatch, while Visual Matching places simulated robots and interactive objects against inpainted real-scene backgrounds and adjusts their appearance. Google Robot and WidowX task setups are implemented in SAPIEN. The framework assesses policy misranking through real-world success-rate margins using Mean Maximum Rank Violation, alongside Pearson correlation. Across six policy checkpoints in three Google Robot task groups, average rank violation is 0.056 for Visual Matching, 0.143 for Variant Aggregation over randomized visual environments, and 0.375 for validation action mean squared error. A complementary behavioral check finds greater simulated arm-texture sensitivity in Octo-Base than RT-1-X, a relative difference supported by subsequent real robot arm-wrapping experiments. These comparisons support simulation as a policy-development signal in the tested, mainly rigid-body settings, with agreement assessed through rankings and policy-dependent behavior.
cases.methods: SIMPLER aligns simulated evaluation with real robot behavior before comparing policies. In SAPIEN implementations of Google Robot and WidowX tasks, system identification replays actions from existing real demonstrations and compares end-effector translation and rotation. Simulated annealing adjusts controller stiffness and damping to reduce trajectory mismatch without collecting new demonstrations. Visual Matching then composites segmented simulated robots and interactive objects with inpainted real backgrounds and adjusts textures to match appearance. Variant Aggregation offers an alternative by averaging evaluations across randomized visual environments. Existing generalist policies undergo paired real and simulated evaluation. Agreement is measured with Mean Maximum Rank Violation: each policy receives its largest real-world success-rate margin among pairs misordered in simulation, and these penalties are averaged across policies. Lower values indicate better ordering; Pearson correlation provides a complementary measure.
cases.results: Visual Matching provides closer agreement with real-world policy rankings than either Variant Aggregation or validation action mean squared error in the Google Robot comparison. Across six checkpoints and three task groups, average Mean Maximum Rank Violation is 0.056, 0.143, and 0.375, respectively; this metric penalizes misordering by real-world success-rate margins, with lower values indicating better agreement. Corresponding mean Pearson correlations are 0.924, 0.778, and 0.308, reinforcing the ordering comparison without equating correlation with exact success-rate reproduction. A complementary check tests whether simulated visual sensitivity corresponds to physical behavior: simulation indicates greater arm-texture sensitivity in Octo-Base than RT-1-X, and new real robot arm-wrapping experiments support that relative difference. The evidence concerns relative ranking and policy-specific visual sensitivity in the evaluated setups.

notes.abstract: Selected S01-S05 to connect evaluation gaps with control alignment, visual composition, and margin-aware ranking; S07 and S09 supply ranking and behavioral evidence. Read-back identifies an evaluation framework, not a policy, and keeps the numerical comparison within six checkpoints and three Google Robot task groups.
notes.methods: Selected S02-S06 to explain how action replay and visual matching prepare paired evaluation. Read-back distinguishes controller identification from policy training, specifies the worst-margin-then-average ranking metric, and preserves randomized visual aggregation as an alternative rather than part of Visual Matching.
notes.results: Selected S07 (Table I) and S09 (Figs. 8-9) to connect ranking agreement with a physically checked sensitivity prediction. Read-back keeps rank-violation and correlation values distinct from success rates and treats arm wrapping as support for relative sensitivity, not exact simulation fidelity.
